newsitem.title: JAPAN: Trade figures unlikely to spark rise in yen.
newsitem.headline: Trade figures unlikely to spark rise in yen.

text.p: A surprise increase in Japan's trade surplus is unlikely to prompt U.S. officials to push the yen higher in a bid to help American companies compete, traders and analysts said on Wednesday.

While a higher yen would normally help reduce the trade gap, traders and analysts said it would be a dangerous step for U.S. policymakers since it would make U.S. securities less attractive to Japanese investors and could cause a stampede in already nervous financial markets.

"A strong dollar is a lifeline for the United States, which has relied on its budgetary financing from overseas investors," said Shuji Ayabe, deputy general manager and head of the foreign exchange department at Fuji Bank Ltd.
"It is highly unlikely they will abandon the policy for the sake of the trade issue now," he added.

The Finance Ministry said on Wednesday that the November trade surplus clicked up a marginal 0.2 percent to 675.19 billion yen ($5.92 billion) as a weaker yen boosted Japanese exports, especially of cars.
It was the first time in two years that the trade surplus had risen, which surprised experts.
The politically sensitive surplus with the United States, meanwhile, leapt more than 30 percent, reflecting an increase in automotive exports.
Private economists had forecast a hefty drop of around 28 percent in the overall surplus, continuing the long-standing declining trend.
The dollar fell to 113.30 yen on the data but was well-supported by dollar buying interest from Japanese investors.
Currency dealers reacted calmly to the news, saying they felt an increase in Japan's trade surplus was not the centre of concerns in the foreign exchange market now.
"I don't think just one month's figure would prompt any major shift in U.S. trade policy toward Japan," said Toshihiko Masaki, foreign exchange manager for Citibank in Tokyo.

"The main theme of the dollar/yen market remains the capital flow out of Japan into the United States, rather than bilateral trade tensions, and this is lending constant support to the dollar," he added.
Japan is a huge investor in U.S. Treasuries. The government alone is reckoned to hold most of its $217 billion of external reserves in U.S. government securities.
Fuji Bank's Ayabe said operators were paying more attention to Japan's trade surplus when the exchange rate for the dollar was around 100 yen.
But unless U.S. authorities start speaking out about their concerns about a rising trade deficit with Japan, a sharp rise in the yen is unlikely to occur, he added.
"Instead the prospects that Japan's absolutely low interest rates will last for a long period are expected to keep the yen weak," he added.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reiterated recently that the Clinton administration has no plans to change its strong-dollar policy, despite stepped-up criticism from U.S. manufacturing companies. A strong dollar helps keep inflation down since it lowers the cost of imports.

Analysts also warned that any change in signals from the United States over currencies could threaten already jittery financial markets, especially if the comments prompted a pullout of U.S. funds by Japanese and other foreign investors. ($1=114)
